title: Farewell to Sobia on her wedding day
takeaway: May God protect you. Be patient, be kind, and you'll find peace.
scene: Another wedding farewell, this time in Urdu, for a daughter of the family named Sobia (perhaps a granddaughter or niece). As she leaves for her new home, the poet blesses her and gives advice.
context: Traditional advice. This is how many parents of the poet's generation spoke to a daughter on her wedding day. The old phrase 'majazi khuda' ('earthly lord') for a husband is a cultural saying of that time, not a religious teaching.

original: بابل کے گھر کی زینت خوشیوں کا باب ہے تو
غزالہ کے گلستاں کا اعلیٰ گلاب ہے تو
transliteration: Baabul ke ghar ki zeenat, khushiyon ka baab hai tu
Ghazaala ke gulistaan ka aala gulaab hai tu
translation: You are the jewel of your father's house, a chapter of happiness;
you are the finest rose in Ghazala's garden.
couplets.story: She has been the pride of her father's house and a source of happiness. She's the most beautiful rose in her mother Ghazala's garden.

original: شرم و حیا کی پتلی عزت مآب ہے تو
اک طرز زندگی کا اعلیٰ نصاب ہے تو
transliteration: Sharm-o-hayaa ki putli, izzat-maab hai tu
Ik tarz-e-zindagi ka aala nisaab hai tu
translation: You are the very image of modesty, and worthy of honour;
you are the finest lesson in a way of living.
couplets.story: She is modest and deserves respect. The way she lives is an example others could learn from.

original: آباد تیرے دم سے یہ گلستاں سدا ہو
حامی تیرا نبی ہو حافظ تیرا خدا ہو
transliteration: Aabaad tere dam se yeh gulistaan sada ho
Haami tera Nabi ho, haafiz tera Khuda ho
translation: May this garden always flourish because of you;
may the Prophet be your supporter, and God your protector.
couplets.story: He prays that her new home will always flourish because of her, that the Prophet will stand by her, and that God will keep her safe.

original: میکے کو دے کے آنسو ڈولی میں جب چڑھے گی
بہنوں سے تو بچھڑ کر جب دور جا بسے گی
transliteration: Maike ko de ke aansoo doli mein jab charhegi
Behnon se tu bichhar kar jab door ja basegi
translation: When you climb into the wedding palanquin, leaving tears behind in your parents' home,
when you're parted from your sisters and go to live far away,
couplets.story: When she gets into the wedding carriage, everyone at home will be crying. She'll be leaving her sisters and moving far away.

original: اس وقت تم پہ لازم صبر و رضا ہے بیٹی
سچ ہے کہ صابروں پر راضی خدا ہے بیٹی
transliteration: Us waqt tum pe laazim sabr-o-razaa hai beti
Sach hai ke saabiron par raazi Khuda hai beti
translation: at that time, daughter, you must be patient and accepting.
It's true, daughter: God is pleased with those who are patient.
couplets.story: At that moment, she'll need to be patient and accept what God has planned. God loves people who are patient.

original: ثوبیہ بیٹی سن لو اک بات یاد رکھنا
بابل کا غم بھلا کر تم دل کو شاد رکھنا
transliteration: Sobia beti sun lo, ik baat yaad rakhna
Baabul ka gham bhula kar tum dil ko shaad rakhna
translation: Sobia, my daughter, listen, and remember one thing:
put aside the sorrow of leaving your father, and keep your heart happy.
couplets.story: He asks her to remember one thing: don't stay sad about leaving your father's house. Keep your heart happy.

original: ساس و سسر ہیں تیرے ماں باپ یاد رکھنا
با ادب ان سے رہنا با مراد رکھنا
transliteration: Saas-o-susar hain tere maan baap yaad rakhna
Ba-adab un se rehna, ba-muraad rakhna
translation: Remember: your mother-in-law and father-in-law are your mother and father now.
Be respectful to them, and you'll find what you hope for.
couplets.story: Treat your husband's parents like your own mother and father. Be respectful to them, and good things will come to you.

original: ہے قول با ادب جو با نصیب ہو گا
وہ کامراں ہو گا سب کا حبیب ہو گا
transliteration: Hai qaul, ba-adab jo, ba-naseeb hoga
Woh kaamraan hoga, sab ka habeeb hoga
translation: There's a saying: whoever is respectful will be fortunate;
they'll succeed, and everyone will love them.
couplets.story: As the saying goes, people who are polite and respectful end up lucky. They do well, and everyone loves them.

original: ثوبیہ بیٹی میری اک اور ہے ہدایت
جیٹھ سے پیار کرنا اور نند سے عنایت
transliteration: Sobia beti meri, ik aur hai hidaayat
Jeth se pyaar karna aur nand se inaayat
translation: Sobia, my daughter, here's one more piece of advice:
be loving to your husband's brother, and kind to his sister.
couplets.story: One more thing: be loving to your husband's brothers and kind to his sisters.

original: اپنے مجازی رب کی کرنا ہمیشہ عزت
پھر پا سکو گی ہر اک زندگی کی راحت
transliteration: Apne majaazi Rab ki karna hamesha izzat
Phir pa sakogi har ik zindagi ki raahat
translation: Always honour your husband (in the old phrase, 'your earthly lord');
then you'll find every comfort life can give.
couplets.story: Always respect your husband. If you do, the poet says, you'll find peace and comfort in every part of life.

original: حاصل سکون ہو گا ہے راحت بندگی میں
معراج ہو گی حاصل خدمت کی چاشنی میں
transliteration: Haasil sakoon hoga, hai raahat bandagi mein
Meraaj hogi haasil khidmat ki chaashni mein
translation: You'll find peace, for there is comfort in worshipping God;
you'll reach the heights through the sweetness of serving others.
couplets.story: He ends with the deepest advice. Real peace comes from worshipping God, and the highest joy comes from the sweetness of serving other people.

deeper: The final couplet holds the spiritual centre: 'there is comfort in worship (bandagi)' and 'the heights (meraj) come through the sweetness of service'. This is a Sufi idea, that serving others for God's sake lifts the soul. 'God is pleased with the patient' echoes the Qur'an: 'God is with those who are patient' (2:153).
why: A father's farewell full of love. It also shows the traditional family values of its time, which readers today may see differently.
prompt: The poem says the highest joy comes from serving others. Have you ever felt that?
notes: Sobia's exact relation to the poet isn't stated; Ghazala is presumably her mother.
Couplet 10 uses the traditional phrase 'majazi khuda/Rab' for a husband. It is a cultural expression, not a religious claim, and the app should explain it as a phrase from its time.
